newsitem.title: USA: MedCare creating incontinence treatment network.
newsitem.headline: MedCare creating incontinence treatment network.

text.p: MedCare Technologies Inc, which has developed a behavior modification program to treat patients suffering from bladder control problems, said Thursday it is creating a network of sites to offer its services which it hopes will number 100 within five years.

These plans may be accelerated if current talks with a large hospital administration firm and physician management companies result in agreements, MedCare president Harmel Rayat said in a telephone interview from the company's offices in Lisle, Ill.

"We are waiting for a proposal from a large hospital administration firm interested in putting our program in one site at one of its hospitals to test it as a precursor to a national launch," Rayat said. He did not identify the company.

But MedCare is not depending on outside forces to fuel its growth. He said the company is currently in talks with investment firms seeking to raise between $5 million and $10 million in 1997 through a private placement in the next few months.

Meanwhile, Medcare will open a treatment center in Kansas City, Mo., in mid-November. Its other center, which has been open in Oklahoma City, Okla., for a few weeks, continues to attract a growing number of patients who have chosen not to undergo conventional treatments such as drugs or surgery.
According to industry experts, urinary incontinence affects some 25 million people. It is a $16 billion market and accounts for almost half of all nursing home admissions.
MedCare's behavior modification training costs about $200 for each session of therapy and, on average, a patient attends about six to eight one-hour sessions.
MedCare's treatment does not require approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and is covered by most health insurance plans.

MedCare has plans for clinics in Illinois, Florida, New York, Texas, Arizona and California which will be located in existing doctors' offices. The clinics "will mark MedCare's transition from a development stage company to a commercial vendor of its medical protocol for treating bladder control problems," the company said in a statement Thursday.

And while profits may not be generated near term, Rayat said he sees a turnaround. "I expect next year will see a break-even at best for the whole year, and going into 1998 it will be a very profitable firm," he said.
"Our plans call for over 100 sites within five years and that is very conservative," Rayat said. "We don't want to be a small regional player. We want to offer service on national basis," he said.
Shares of MedCare, which went public about a year ago, were trading off 1/16 at 4-13/16.
